summary.text: Son of Zeus and Danae — or of a mortal scandal in one tradition — the hero who crossed the sea in a chest, slew the Gorgon with the gods' gifts, freed Andromeda from the sea-beast, and founded Mycenae after the discus that fulfilled his grandfather's oracle.

chapters.title: The golden shower
chapters.text: Acrisius king of Argos, warned that his daughter's son would kill him, shut Danae in a bronze chamber — yet Zeus came to her as a shower of gold, and she bore Perseus. Apollodorus notes an alternative: that her uncle Proetus seduced her and the brothers went to war. Either way the child was born, and the king cast mother and infant into the sea in a wooden chest.

chapters.title: Seriphos and the Gorgon
chapters.text: The chest came ashore on Seriphos, where Dictys the fisherman reared the boy while King Polydectes lusted after Danae. To rid himself of the protector, Polydectes feigned a wedding and demanded horse-gifts; Perseus promised the Gorgon's head instead. Hermes and Athena gave him the sickle, the kibisis, the cap of Hades, and winged sandals; from the Graeae he learned the way to the Gorgons and cut off Medusa's head — Pegasus and Chrysaor springing from her neck.

chapters.title: Andromeda and the return
chapters.text: Flying over Ethiopia he saw Andromeda chained for her mother's boast against the Nereids; he turned Cetus to stone with the Gorgon's face and won the princess. Returning to Seriphos he petrified Polydectes and set Dictys on the throne. At Larisa a discus thrown in the funeral games struck Acrisius by accident — the oracle fulfilled. Perseus exchanged Argos for Tiryns with Megapenthes and built Mycenae; whether he died in peace or by vengeance the poets disagree.
